```{r setup}
#| echo: false
#| message: false

library(tidyverse)
library(easystats)
library(patchwork)
mytheme <- function(sz = 30) {
  theme_gray(base_size = sz) + 
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
}
# Make mytheme the default rather than relying on every plot remembering
# `+ mytheme`. Plots built by other packages -- plot(), check_model(),
# ggeffects -- never get a manual `+ mytheme` and were rendering at
# ggplot's 11pt default, which reads as tiny next to the 40px slide text.
theme_set(mytheme())
```


# Overview

## Motivation {.fs90}

- So far, we have always fit [straight lines]{.b} between $y$ and $x$ variables

- But sometimes the correct functional form is [curved]{.b .red} in some way

- If we fit a straight line anyway, our results may be very biased

```{r, fig.width=9, fig.height=3}
set.seed(2023)
df1 <- tibble(
  x = runif(100, -5, 5), 
  y1 = 0.2 + 1.2*x + rnorm(100, 0, 1)
)
df2 <- tibble(
  x = runif(100, -5, 5), 
  y2 = 0.2 + 1.2*x - 0.5*x^2 + rnorm(100, 0, 2)
)

p1 <- ggplot(df1, aes(x, y1)) + 
  geom_point(size = 2) + 
  # geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "red", linewidth = 1.5,
  #             formula = y ~ x + I(x^2)) +
  # geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "blue", linewidth = 1.5,
  #             formula = y ~ x) +
  mytheme(20)
p2 <- ggplot(df2, aes(x, y2)) + 
  geom_point(size = 2, color = "red") + 
  # geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "red", linewidth = 1.5,
  #             formula = y ~ x + I(x^2)) +
  # geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "blue", linewidth = 1.5,
  #             formula = y ~ x) +
  mytheme(20)
  
(p1 | p2)
```

## Linear regression

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| collapse: true
#| message: false

fit <- lm(y2 ~ x, data = df2) # data from right panel of slide 3

model_parameters(fit)

r2(fit)
```

## Visualizing the model

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

library(ggeffects)
plot(predict_response(fit, terms = "x"), show_data = TRUE)
```

```{r}
#| message: false
library(ggeffects)
plot(predict_response(fit, terms = "x"), show_data = TRUE, dot_size = 3) + mytheme()
```

## Assumption checking

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

check_model(fit, check = "linearity")
```

```{r}
see:::plot.see_check_model(check_model(fit, check = "linearity", panel = FALSE))$NCV + 
  mytheme() + 
  theme(
    plot.title.position = "plot",
    plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0, size = 22),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(hjust = 0, size = 20)
  )
```

## Conclusions {.fs90}

- Linear regression did not work well for predicting $y_2$

- The functional form diagnostic looked bad for the latter

- The $R^2$ for the latter was worse than we could do

::: {.fragment}
- We need to change our functional form!

- We need to allow a curve in our function

- This is what polynomial regression does
:::

# Polynomial Regression

## Power polynomials {.fs70}

- LM can handle simple curves through **power polynomial** transformations!

- We will add predictors that are *power transformations* of other predictors

$$\hat{y} = b_0 + b_1 \color{red}{x^1} + b_2 \color{red}{x^2} + \cdots + b_d \color{red}{x^d}$$

- Each term has a **degree** equal to its exponent
    + e.g., $x^1$ is the *first* degree term and $x^2$ is the *second* degree term
    + Note that $x^1=x$ and $x^0=1$, which can be thought of as the intercept
    + The term with the highest exponent is the **highest degree term**
    + All other terms are referred to as the **lower degree terms**


## Number of bends {.fs90}

- The highest degree term determines the curve's overall shape
    + The number of bends is equal to $(d-1)$

```{r, fig.width=10, fig.height=4}
d1 <- tibble(x = seq(-3, 3, .1), y = x^1) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x, y)) + 
  geom_line(linewidth = 2, color = "darkblue") + 
  labs(title = "Linear (d=1)") +
  mytheme(20) +
  theme(axis.text = element_blank())
d2 <- tibble(x = seq(-3, 3, .1), y = x^2) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x, y)) + 
  geom_line(linewidth = 2, color = "darkblue") +
  labs(title = "Quadratic (d=2)") +
  mytheme(20) +
  theme(axis.text = element_blank())
d3 <- tibble(x = seq(-3, 3, .1), y = -5*x + x^3) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x, y)) + 
  geom_line(linewidth = 2, color = "darkblue") +
  labs(title = "Cubic (d=3)") +
  mytheme(20) +
  theme(axis.text = element_blank())

(d1 | d2 | d3)
```
    

## Direction of curvature {.fs90}

- The sign $(\pm)$ of the curve's highest degree term's slope<br>determines its **direction of curvature** (i.e., up or down)

```{r, fig.width=10, fig.height=4}
qp <- tibble(x = seq(-10, 10, 1), y = x^2) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x, y)) + 
  geom_line(linewidth = 2, color = "darkblue") + 
  labs(title = expression(paste("y = ", +1*x^2))) +
  mytheme(20) +
  theme(axis.text = element_blank())
qn <- tibble(x = seq(-10, 10, 1), y = -x^2) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x, y)) + 
  geom_line(linewidth = 2, color = "darkblue") +
  labs(title = expression(paste("y = ", -1*x^2))) +
  mytheme(20) +
  theme(axis.text = element_blank())
cp <- tibble(x = seq(-10, 10, 1), y = x^3) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x, y)) + 
  geom_line(linewidth = 2, color = "darkblue") +
  labs(title = expression(paste("y = ", +1*x^3))) +
  mytheme(20) +
  theme(axis.text = element_blank())
cn <- tibble(x = seq(-10, 10, 1), y = -x^3) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x, y)) + 
  geom_line(linewidth = 2, color = "darkblue") + 
  labs(title = expression(paste("y = ", -1*x^3))) +
  mytheme(20) +
  theme(axis.text = element_blank())

(qp | qn | cp | cn)
```

# Quadratic Regression

## Expanding the equation {.fs90}

- A quadratic relationship requires two predictors to represent $x$

$$\hat{y} = b_0 + b_1 x^1 + b_2 x^2$$

- The **highest** degree coefficient determines the overall shape
    + $b_2$: Does the curve bend up $(+)$, down $(-)$, or not at all $(0)$?

::: {.pv2}
- The **lower** degree coefficients fine-tune the position and shape
    + $b_1$: What is the slope of the curve's tangent line at $x=0$?
    + $b_0$: What is the intercept of the curve's tangent line at $x=0$?

:::

## Quadratic regression 1

- We use the `I()` function to do math inside the formula

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| collapse: true

fit1b <- lm(y1 ~ x + I(x^2), data = df1)

model_parameters(fit1b)

r2(fit1b)
```

::: {.fs90}
The $x^2$ slope is NOT significant, so the curve is NOT needed
:::


## Visualizing the model

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

plot(predict_response(fit1b, terms = "x"), show_data = TRUE)
```

```{r}
#| message: false

plot(predict_response(fit1b, terms = "x"), show_data = TRUE, dot_size = 3) + mytheme()
```

## Assumption checking

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

check_model(fit1b, check = "linearity")
```

```{r}
see:::plot.see_check_model(check_model(fit1b, check = "linearity", panel = FALSE))$NCV + 
  mytheme() + 
  theme(
    plot.title.position = "plot",
    plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0, size = 22),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(hjust = 0, size = 20)
  )
```

## Quadratic regression 2

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| collapse: true

fit2b <- lm(y2 ~ x + I(x^2), data = df2)

model_parameters(fit2b)

r2(fit2b)
```

- The $x^2$ slope is significant, so the curve is needed!
- Because the slope is negative, it will bend downward


## Visualizing the model

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

plot(predict_response(fit2b, terms = "x"), show_data = TRUE)
```

```{r}
#| message: false

plot(predict_response(fit2b, terms = "x"), show_data = TRUE, dot_size = 3) + mytheme()
```

## Assumption checking

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

check_model(fit2b, check = "linearity")
```

```{r}
see:::plot.see_check_model(check_model(fit2b, check = "linearity", panel = FALSE))$NCV + 
  mytheme() + 
  theme(
    plot.title.position = "plot",
    plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0, size = 22),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(hjust = 0, size = 20)
  )
```


## Visualizing the tangent line

```{r}
ggplot(df2, aes(x = x, y = y2)) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5) + 
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x + I(x^2), linewidth = 1.5) +
  geom_abline(
    slope = 1.27, 
    intercept = -0.16, 
    color = "orange", 
    linewidth = 2,
    alpha = 4/5
  ) +
  annotate(
    geom = "label",
    x = 0,
    y = -12,
    label = "y = –0.16 + 1.27x",
    color = "orange",
    size = 7
  ) +
  annotate(
    geom = "label",
    x = 0,
    y = -16,
    label = "y = –0.16 + 1.27x – 0.50x²",
    color = "blue",
    size = 7
  ) +
  mytheme()
```


## Calculating extrema

- It may be useful to know the maximum or minimum values

::: {.columns}
::: {.column}

What value of $x$ gives the<br>most extreme value of $y$?

$$x_m = \frac{-b_1}{2b_2}$$

:::
::: {.column}
What is the most extreme value of $y$ in the function?

$$\hat{y}_m = \frac{4 b_2 b_0 - b_1^2}{4 b_2}$$

:::
:::

## Calculating extrema {.fs90}

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| collapse: true

model_parameters(fit2b)

b_0 <- -0.16
b_1 <-  1.27
b_2 <- -0.50

x_m <- (-b_1) / (2 * b_2)
x_m

yhat_m <- ((4 * b_2 * b_0) - b_1^2) / (4 * b_2)
yhat_m
```

## Visualizing extrema

```{r}
ggplot(df2, aes(x = x, y = y2)) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5) + 
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x + I(x^2), linewidth = 1.5) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.64645, color = "orange", linewidth = 1.5, alpha = 4/5) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1.27, color = "orange", linewidth = 1.5, alpha = 4/5) +
  annotate("label", x = 1.27, y = -17.5, label = "1.27", size = 7, color = "orange") +
  annotate("label", x = -3.75, y = 0.64645, label = "0.65", size = 7, color = "orange") +
  mytheme()
```



# Adding Predictors

## Adding another predictor {.fs90}

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| collapse: true
#| message: false
#| replace_path: ["../../data/", ""]

library(tidyverse)
salaries <- read_csv("../../data/salaries.csv")

fit3 <- lm(salary ~ yrs.since.phd + I(yrs.since.phd^2) + sex, data = salaries)

model_parameters(fit3)
```

- The effects of `yrs.since.phd` are significant controlling for sex

- The effect of `sex` is significant controlling for `yrs.since.phd` and its square


## Visualizing the model {.fs90}

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

plot(predict_response(fit3, terms = c("yrs.since.phd", "sex")), show_data = TRUE)
```

```{r}
plot(predict_response(fit3, terms = c("yrs.since.phd", "sex")), show_data = TRUE) + mytheme()
```

## Adding moderation {.fs90}

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| collapse: true
#| message: false

fit4 <- lm(
  salary ~ yrs.since.phd + I(yrs.since.phd^2) + sex + 
    yrs.since.phd:sex + I(yrs.since.phd^2):sex, 
  data = salaries
)

model_parameters(fit4)
```

- The effects of `yrs.since.phd` are not moderated by sex

## Visualizing the model

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

plot(predict_response(fit4, terms = c("yrs.since.phd", "sex")))
```

```{r}
plot(predict_response(fit4, terms = c("yrs.since.phd", "sex"))) + mytheme()
```


# Closing Thoughts

## Consider the range

- You may only see *part* of the curve in your sample!

```{r,echo = FALSE, fig.width=8, fig.height=4}

p1 <- tibble(x = seq(-10, 0, 1), y = -x^2) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x, y)) + geom_line(size = 2, color = "darkblue") +
  labs(y = expression(paste("y = ", -x^2)), x = NULL) + 
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(-10, -5, 0, 5, 10)) +
  mytheme(20) + 
  theme(axis.text = element_blank())

p2 <- tibble(x = seq(-5, 5, 1), y = -x^2) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x, y)) + geom_line(size = 2, color = "darkblue") +
  labs(y = NULL, x = NULL) + 
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(-10, -5, 0, 5, 10)) +
  mytheme(20) + 
  theme(axis.text = element_blank())

p3 <- tibble(x = seq(0, 10, 1), y = -x^2) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x, y)) + geom_line(size = 2, color = "darkblue") +
  labs(y = NULL, x = NULL) + 
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(-10, -5, 0, 5, 10)) +
  mytheme(20) + 
  theme(axis.text = element_blank())

p4 <- tibble(x = seq(-10, 0, 1), y = x^2) |>  
  ggplot(aes(x, y)) + geom_line(size = 2, color = "darkblue") +
  labs(y = expression(paste("y = ", x^2))) + 
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(-10, -5, 0, 5, 10)) +
  mytheme(20) + 
  theme(axis.text.y = element_blank())

p5 <- tibble(x = seq(-5, 5, 1), y = x^2) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x, y)) + geom_line(size = 2, color = "darkblue") +
  labs(y = NULL) + 
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(-10, -5, 0, 5, 10)) +
  mytheme(20) + 
  theme(axis.text.y = element_blank())

p6 <- tibble(x = seq(0, 10, 1), y = x^2) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x, y)) + geom_line(size = 2, color = "darkblue") +
  labs(y = NULL) + 
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(-10, -5, 0, 5, 10)) +
  mytheme(20) + 
  theme(axis.text.y = element_blank())

((p1 | p2 | p3) / (p4 | p5 | p6)) + plot_annotation(theme = mytheme())
```

## Advice {.fs90}

- Models with higher degrees are more flexible
    + But they may overfit (fail to generalize)
    + They will be harder to interpret and justify
    
- **Theory** should be used to decide between shapes
    + Quadratics can model processes with best/worst regions
    + Cubics can model opponent processes and regulation
    
- Centering your $x$ variable is very helpful here
    + Also see `poly()` for orthogonal polynomials

- Don't omit the lower degree terms/coefficients
